newsitem.title: UK: More evidence found of viral link to MS.
newsitem.headline: More evidence found of viral link to MS.

text.p: Danish researchers said on Friday they had found more evidence of a viral link to multiple sclerosis (MS), and said a common type of herpes virus could be to blame.
Dr Sven Haahr and colleagues at the University of Aarhus in Denmark reported a cluster of eight people with MS living in the village of Fjelso, which has 74 families.
The MS victims all went to the same elementary school for seven years, all had been Scouts and four were related.

Writing in a letter to the Lancet medical journal, they said this strengthened the theory that a virus might be to blame, and nominated Epstein-Barr virus, the herpes virus that causes "glandular fever" (also known as mononucleosis or the "kissing disease").

"Our group has previously put forward a dual infection hypothesis for MS, suggesting that infection with a more or less widespread MS retrovirus' is a prerequisite for development of MS, but MS develops only or especially in those who are infected with Epstein-Barr virus around puberty or later in life and who are genetically susceptible," they wrote.
They said they were now testing the villagers to see if they were infected with the virus.
Multiple sclerosis is an autoimmune disease in which the body's immune system attacks the insulating myelin around nerves in the brain and spinal cord. There is no cure.

But steroids are often used to treat the symptoms. In a second Lancet study, Dr David Barnes and colleagues at Atkinson Morley's Hospital in London said they found that oral steroids worked just as well as injections, which would make the treatment easier on both doctors and patients.
Several other studies have linked MS with herpes viruses, the family of viruses that cause cold sores, chickenpox and shingles.
Earlier this month Belgian scientists said MS was caused by antibodies against herpes-virus 6. HHV-6 causes roseola, which is marked by a red rash and feverish convulsions in young children.
A study earlier this year in the International Journal of Cancer linked the Epstein-Barr virus with Hodgkin's disease.
A search is on for a vaccine against herpes viruses which infect nearly everybody and stay in the body forever.
